newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN delays Cambodia entry, but Burma still on.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN delays Cambodia entry, but Burma still on.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) announced on Thursday it had postponed Cambodia's membership but would still admit Burma and Laos later this month.

In a joint statement after an emergency meeting on the Cambodian crisis, ASEAN also said it still recognised Prince Norodom Ranariddh as co-premier of Cambodia despite his ouster by rival Second Prime Minister Hun Sen after weekend fighting between their forces.

"ASEAN will continue to regard Ranariddh as co-premier of Cambodia," Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told reporters after the meeting. In Phnom Penh, Hun Sen told reporters before the decision to delay membership was announced that Cambodia's troubles were "our internal business".
"ASEAN countries must let us solve our problems on our own," he said. "Please stay out of our internal business."

Hun Sen denied he had staged a coup d'etat and said Ranariddh, in Paris when the fighting began, could return to Phnom Penh "to face court". He did not say what sort of legal proceedings Ranariddh might face if he returned.
Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which also includes Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded in clashes between forces loyal to Hun Sen and those with Ranardiddh last weekend.

ASEAN's statement reiterated the grouping's long-stated policy of not interfering in a neighbouring country's internal affairs, but said the use of force in the feud between Hun Sen and Ranariddh made it necessary to delay Cambodia's entry. "While reaffirming the commitment to the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of the other states, (the foreign ministers) decided that in t he light of unfortunate circumstances which have resulted from the use of force, the wisest course of action is to delay the admission of Cambodia into ASEAN until a later date," the statement said.

The meeting decided that Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas and Philippines Foreign Minister Domingo Siazon should fly to Beijing soon to meet Cambodia's head of state, King Norodom Sihanouk, over ways to resolve the crisis.
"We'll get in touch with his majesty King Sihanouk and the indication is the earlier the better. After that, we'll get in touch with the co-premiers," Siazon told reporters.

Alatas said delaying Cambodia's admission was "a practical decison". "We did not pass judgment on who is right, who is wrong, who is legitimate or who is illegitimate or whether there was a coup d'etat," he told reporters after the meeting.

ASEAN has maintained that members cannot interfere in each other's domestic affairs, especially when governments of current members range from a communist one-party state in Vietnam, an absolute monarchy in Brunei, an authoritarian government in Indonesia and democracies in Thailand and the Philippines.
ASEAN has a long history of diplomatic involvement in Cambodia. Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was an architect of the accords that Washington said on Tuesday had been ruptured by Hun Sen.
In the 1980s, ASEAN supported a guerrilla coalition that included Ranariddh's faction and the Khmer Rouge against the Vietnamese-backed government in Phnom Penh led by Hun Sen.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington had "given some advice" to ASEAN for its meeting. He refused to say specifically what the advice was, but said it was important for countries with an interest in Cambodia "to speak out about what is acceptable and what is not acceptable".
Western diplomats expressed disappointment that ASEAN passed up the opportunity to defer Burma's membership as well.

"ASEAN had the opportunity to show it was cognisant of concerns about internal security and human rights in Burma and Cambodia and could have sent some clear signals to the international community," said one.
